Introducing the "The State of Our Climate" R Shiny App: Our team at the University of Washington has been hard at work on our first R Shiny App project, and we're thrilled to unveil "The State of Our Climate"! Check it out here: https://lnkd.in/gTHxM5ZE Our app focuses on the critical aspects of average temperatures and velocity of temperature change. By analyzing these factors using time series temperature data from UC Berkeley, we've gained invaluable insights that contribute to a newfound understanding of the global climate crisis. Major Takeaways: - Regional Disparities: We've aggregated average temperature patterns by cities and countries. Certain areas have experienced accelerated temperature growth, driving the climate crisis. The correlation between emissions and rising temperatures underscores the need for global collaboration. - Temporal Dynamics: Our Velocity of Temperature Change Over Time scatter plot highlights the accelerating speed of temperature shifts. Zooming into specific time frames reveals rapid temperature changes, calling for urgent policies to address this trend. - Customizable Analysis: Our Shiny app empowers users with interactive widgets to tailor their exploration. Whether it's tracking temperature trends over time or exploring each region in more depth, users can derive insights aligned with their goals, driving informed decisions for positive climate action. Many thanks to my amazing team members for their dedication and hard work: - Derek : Temperature Velocity and World Maps implementation, coauthoring app text. - Alicia : World Maps by city visualization. - Sierra : Coauthoring app text. - Myself: Repository setup, Temperature Change visualization, CSS styling, and code debugging. I invite you to join us in getting curious about climate change, uncovering insights, and advocating for systemic change. Spent the weekend at the Carnegie Mellon University AI Agent Hackathon planning to compete as a team of four. But after the event kicked off, we gravitated toward completely different problems. We split into two duos, built completely separate projects, and ended up taking home 2 of the 3 total prizes. 🏆 Grand Prize: Eric Jin and I built DisputeForge, a Reg E-compliant payment dispute resolution agent. Our design philosophy was simple: the differentiator is the harness, not the prompt. We built out a multi-layered LangGraph architecture focused on control and orchestration, integrating custom tools, deterministic rule-engine evaluators, and state checkpointing. By offloading compliance and routing entirely to the harness, our final eval suite hit 93.3% accuracy and 100% escalation recall. 🚀 Most Ambitious: Sam Mathew and Darren Pinto built FieldOps, a real-time multi-agent AI system for mass casualty incident command. Six specialized agents, handling triage, hospital routing, dispatch logistics, and pre-arrival notifications, coordinate through a shared incident state to help field commanders make faster, safer decisions under pressure. Super fun weekend building with friends and watching everyone succeed. Huge thank you to Bo Xie and the CMU Data Science Club for hosting, Capital One for sponsoring, and judges Aditya Singh , Ayushman S. , and Peter Carragher for the feedback! Recently at CMU’s ProdHacks (hosted by CMUBTG ), Rushabh Jain , Darren Pinto , and I took home 1st place in the main Product Track and People’s Choice across both undergrad and graduate teams. We built a consent-first safety product that addresses a real tension many students face: families want reassurance, and students want autonomy. Existing tools often force an all-or-nothing tradeoff (always-on tracking vs. no safety net). Our approach is “safety without surveillance”: private by default, with location shared only when it actually matters (during an incident or explicit opt-in moments) with layered escalation so the right people get notified in the right order. Huge thanks to Minh Nguyen Do for hosting and running an awesome event, to the judges Harish Parmar and Sanket Patil from SAP for the thoughtful feedback, and to CMU BTG for building a space where students can ship real products fast. 1500 builders. 1 winner. Last weekend, my team won the Grand Prize (1st place in the Education track) at NexHacks , one of the largest hackathons in the world. The problem we tackled? Sports coaching is often gated behind expensive private sessions. Together, my teammate Eric Jin and I built Swish: a basketball AI form coach meant to democratize interactive coaching. We built Swish with TensorFlow 's MoveNet model to track body keypoints, then simulated a 3D reconstruction of a virtual basketball court as if the player were actually shooting a basketball. We supplemented this technology with real-time feedback via LiveKit & coaching through Overshoot 's video analysis API. Deep-dive on my blog (coming soon): https://lnkd.in/gCPN2UZ4 ...more

We built an autonomous 3D space mapping robot in one week!! Not a simulation. Not a demo script — a real rover that drives and reconstructs the room around it. For Build18, Darren Pinto , Tanay Mishra , Jayden Chen , Jintong Wang , and I built LOLA — a ~$150 mecanum-drive RC rover running on a Raspberry Pi 4. What made it different? We didn’t use an expensive depth camera. Instead, we used CUT3R to reconstruct 3D models from RGB video only (camera intrinsics/extrinsics). We offloaded heavy compute to Google Colab and made the pipeline easy to rerun + reproduce. For autonomy + mapping, we used LiDAR SLAM with Point-to-Line ICP (PL-ICP) (SVD closed-form solve + kd-tree matching), and built a dynamic occupancy grid that we export for planning. Path planning: from that exported occupancy map, we run an RRT-based planner that outputs collision-free waypoint paths (JSON + a path overlay image), and the rover follows the waypoints autonomously. Huge thanks to the Build18 mentors + team for the support throughout the sprint. 🔗 GitHub (open-source): https://lnkd.in/ggybbHXF #Build18 #Robotics #SLAM #PathPlanning #ComputerVision #RaspberryPi #3DReconstruction ...more ...more

Human memory needs sleep to make sense of the day. It replays what happened, strengthens what matters, connects it to what you already know, and lets the rest fade. AI agents never got that part. LLMs are really bad at reasoning. Chain of thought is expensive and internal reasoning circuits are limited. So why not build an architecture specifically for reasoning. That's what Tiny Recursive Models do. They recursively update latent reasoning and answer spaces. And because of this new training and inference procedure we can use smaller models. While Deepseek R1 has ~700 billion parameters it is incapable of playing Sudoko, 0% on sudoko-extreme. A TRM with 7 million parameters achieves 87.4% on the same benchmark. But applying the same weights to the same vectors is deterministic. If we add noise throughout the process we make a Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model, which achieved 98.75% on sudoku-extreme. I explore these tiny models in this notebook submitted to Marimo’s Notebook Challenge 2. I highly recommend the video explainer although I may be biased. This Wednesday, I had the chance to speak at Women Tech Meetup hosted by Dasha Shunina from OpenRouter , in front of 100+ incredible women in tech. It's always really exciting to see so many women building, founding companies, leading teams, and just being genuinely curious about where AI is going. Communities like this matter a lot, and it's always a pleasure to be part of them. We spent a lot of time talking about AI agents, and I also shared how we're thinking about AI deployments at Contour . One thing I strongly believe is that the hard part isn't building another agent. It's giving that agent the right context. Every deployment creates a huge amount of knowledge: requirements, decisions, stakeholder context, edge cases, what worked, what didn't. Most of it ends up scattered across Slack, docs, tickets, or just stays in people's heads. That's why ontology is such an important piece of the puzzle. It's how you turn all of those implementation learnings into something AI can actually reason over, not just search. I also really loved the questions from the audience. They turned into some of the best conversations of the evening. And apparently there are quite a few WisprFlow fans in the room too haha. Huge thank you to Dasha for the invitation and for creating such a unique atmosphere. Looking forward to the next one <3

Yesterday, Aditya Bankoti , Ioli Shrivastava, Berkan M. va, Berkan M. and I placed 2nd at the Dell × NVIDIA AI Hackathon hosted by BuilderBase. We were given < 10 hours and a GB10 powered computer to build a local solution to any problem. So, we built Nazar... Some places just can't put their data in the cloud. Hospitals, ships, air-gapped banks. So when something breaks, one engineer flies out and stares at logs alone at 2am. We built Nazar, a box that does the staring for them. It reads the broken machines, maps out how everything connects, and a local LLM works the case like a detective until it can tell you what broke and how to fix it. every claim it makes is a footnote pointing at a real line in a real file, so you can check its work. Plugging in an ethernet cable is the entire user interface. And, nothing ever leaves the building. I've spent some time during the summer reading "GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA" by Paulo Motta, Ph.D. What stuck with me wasn't another walkthrough of CUDA kernels. It was the engineering mindset behind the book. A few things stood out, as someone who spends a lot of time thinking about performance in modern C++: 1. GPU programming as engineering, not just kernels - Testing with Google Test and Pytest. - Profiling with Nsight Compute. - Knowing when to reach for cuBLAS or Thrust instead of writing a custom kernel. This is how real production systems get built. 2. Hardware understanding over blind offloading. Performance isn't just faster kernels. It's PCIe bandwidth, data transfer sizes, overlapping communication with computation, and knowing where the real bottleneck sits. The same questions we ask when optimizing CPU-bound low-latency systems. 3. The C++/Python bridge Exposing GPU-accelerated C++ libraries to Python, without unnecessary NumPy copies. Increasingly relevant when Python handles orchestration and C++ handles execution. 4. Written for C++ dev, not GPU researchers The examples build up gradually, stay focused on programming, and skip the math barrier that keeps a lot of C++ developers away from GPU work. My takeaway: - Whether you're optimizing a low-latency trading engine or a GPU workload, the principles don't change. - Understand the hardware. Measure before you optimize. - Treat performance as an engineering discipline, not a collection of tricks. Recommended for any C++ developer curious about GPU computing who isn't sure where to start.

Over the last month I "vibe researched" several PhDs' worth of maths results in and around the field I did my research in 25+ years ago (complete with Lean formalization and passable text). This includes a counterexample to a top-5 major conjecture in the field! I assume any active researcher in the field would have done even better. What does this mean for the bar for a "significant" maths contribution going forward? Clearly you can't just give out PhDs for what I did, so the bar must already be much higher today (even if nothing better than 5.6 shows up), not in some kind of distant and hypothetical future. And if the gap between "5.7" and 5.6 is the same size as the gap between 5.6 and 5.5, we are talking mostly superhuman performance in all aspects of maths. We are going to see 50 years' worth of maths progress in the next 2 years, but there won't be nearly enough human mathematicians around to process and understand all of it, let alone figure out how to apply it all or what new questions to ask.

Human Archive (YC W26) builds datasets to model sensorimotor intelligence for robotics and world models. HA-Multi is the largest dataset of manual labor tasks aligning egocentric RGB, stereo depth (IR dot projection), tactile gloves, body IMUs, and wrist cameras. Human intelligence is predominantly embodied, and the internet does not capture it. Every day we perceive the world, apply force, and adapt to noisy real-world environments. Yet no dataset captures this multimodal structure of human interaction with the world at scale. As a result, progress in embodied spatial intelligence has been bottlenecked. To collect data at scale and ensure quality, they build and deploy custom hardware across homes and businesses, then post-process the resulting data through internal QA, anonymization, annotation pipelines, and policy benchmarking. They've already shipped data to frontier research teams and will open-source samples next week. publications.subtitle: Conference on Intelligent Computation in Manufacturing Engineering
publications.description: Today's rapidly evolving industrial landscape and the progressive digitization of production processes require massive amounts of real-time data on the current production and logistical status. This work proposes a multi-modal mobile sensor system that captures and perceives the production facility environment and fits into a standard load carrier, e.g., to be transported using logistic assets and existing transport routes. In contrast to using numerous stationary sensor solutions, the mobile system especially stands out in lot size one production sites, e.g., in aircraft assembly lines. Besides presenting the overall system, we elaborate on possible applications and prototypical demonstrate and evaluate these.

publications.title: BETTY Dataset: A Multi-modal Dataset for Full-Stack Autonomy
publications.subtitle: The International Conference on Robotics and Automation
publications.description: We present the BETTY dataset, a large-scale, multi-modal dataset collected on several autonomous racing vehicles, targeting supervised and self-supervised state estimation, dynamics modeling, motion forecasting, perception, and more. Existing large-scale datasets, especially autonomous vehicle datasets, focus primarily on supervised perception, planning, and motion forecasting tasks. Our work enables multi-modal, data-driven methods by including all sensor inputs and the outputs from the software stack, along with semantic metadata and ground truth information. The dataset encompasses 4 years of data, currently comprising over 13 hours and 32 TB, collected on autonomous racing vehicle platforms. This data spans 6 diverse racing environments, including high-speed oval courses, for single and multi-agent algorithm evaluation in feature-sparse scenarios, as well as high-speed road courses with high longitudinal and lateral accelerations and tight, GPS-denied environments. It captures highly dynamic states, such as 63 m/s crashes, loss of tire traction, and operation at the limit of stability. By offering a large breadth of cross-modal and dynamic data, the BETTY dataset enables the training and testing of full autonomy stack pipelines, pushing the performance of all algorithms to the limits.

publications.title: Leveraging passive monitoring applications in production and intralogistics
publications.subtitle: Conference on Intelligent Computation in Manufacturing Engineering
publications.description: Today's rapidly evolving industrial landscape and the progressive digitization of products, processes, and resources require massive amounts of online data on the current production and logistical status. Fixed-positioned sensor systems have a constrained Field of View (FoV), while a mobile system can significantly extend these, enabling further applications due to the larger observed space. In this work, we elaborate on potential applications that utilize incidentally acquired data from various locations from the perspective of a mobile, vision-based sensor system. We exemplarily demonstrate an application within the scope of capturing and triggering the intralogistics chain with data from a vision-based sensor system that can be carried by an Autonomous Guided Vehicle (AGV).

A constraint in longevity research: aging lacks a clear regulatory pathway. And since all-cause mortality trials for aging are unfeasible - every drug, even those born from aging research, will be tested against a specific disease instead. Because of this bottleneck, the next major milestones for the field are expected in three directions: Path 1: Win disease by disease. Show that a single drug succeeds in separate trials across several age-related diseases, making it hard to deny the drug is acting on aging itself rather than any one condition. Path 2: Test against multiple diseases at once. Successfully test a single drug against several age-related diseases simultaneously in a single trial, directly demonstrating that it acts on aging broadly. Path 3: Change the rules. Get a regulator to approve new trial designs based on surrogate endpoints using functional parameters (like grip strength, walking speed, or cognitive performance), or aging biomarkers (like chronic inflammation levels or epigenetic patterns). To understand this new industry fully, Social Capital partnered with a team of leading researchers to put together a two-part deep dive into longevity biotech and aging research. I'm wrapping up my internship at Scotiabank a little earlier than expected. But before I share what's next, I wanted to reflect on few things I've learned over the past seven months. When I switched majors in my third year of university, I felt like I was behind everyone else. I graduated a semester later than most of my friends, wondering if I was already "late". When I joined the bank as a CX Design Intern in January, I wasn't even sure if I had the skills to do well in my role. I didn't study design. Honestly, I didn't even know what CX was before January. Looking back, I realize I was worrying about the wrong things. 💡 One thing that changed everything for me was simply 𝐚𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬. Since I didn't come from a design background, I reached out to UX designers, service designers, and product designers because I was genuinely curious about their work and wanted to understand how they made their design decisions. Beyond designers, I talked to anyone who was willing to share their experiences. Every person around you has experiences that you can learn from. If you're an intern or just starting your career, don't be afraid of not knowing things. Nobody expects you to know everything. You're new to the company, to the industry, maybe even to corporate life itself. People are usually more than happy to help if they see that you're genuinely curious and willing to learn. 💡 Another thing I learned is to 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐩 𝐰𝐚𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐲𝐨𝐮. If you have capacity (and most interns probably do), ask if there's something you can help with. I looked for ways I could contribute instead of waiting for someone to assign me work. It might start with something small, but if you do it well, people remember and start trusting you with bigger projects, more responsibility, and opportunities you never expected you would have as an intern. That could feel overwhelming sometimes, and there were definitely moments where I looked at my backlog and thought, "Can I actually do this?" But one quote has really stuck with me: "𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐠𝐞." If people keep trusting you with bigger opportunities, it's because they believe you're capable. It pushes you to learn faster, think differently, and grow in ways you probably wouldn't if you stayed comfortable. So 𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞. 💡 One last thing I want to share is this from our EVP: 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐥𝐞𝐬. I wasn't chasing a specific title or trying to fit into the "perfect role". I wanted to become someone who create compelling designs, communicate ideas clearly, take ownership, collaborate across teams, challenge ideas respectfully, and be someone others could rely on. Over time, those small things started adding up. People trusted me with bigger initiatives, asking for my input, and giving me opportunities I never expected to have as an intern. The titles will come. The skills are what stay with you. And that's why I'm wrapping up my internship a little earlier than expected - I'm excited to be continuing my journey at Scotiabank as a Manager, CX Programs & Visual Design. I know it's a big jump, but to me, it reflects my team's belief in my potential. Now it's my turn to stretch, grow, and live up to that trust. So if you're feeling behind or don't feel "qualified enough", don't let that stop you. Be curious. Ask questions. Take initiative. Learn from the people around you. None of this would've been possible without my team - Natasha Mohindra , Andrea Erickson (Huitrón) , Nick Somwaru, Julia Cipollone (Soye) , and everyone in the Client Expereince Management Office and the program.🚀 Thank you for trusting me with meaningful work and creating an environment where I could learn, make mistakes, and grow. I couldn't have asked for a better team to start my career with. Looking forward to this next chapter! ❤️

activity.title: We invited 199 founders to bring an egg to Cancun. They drew faces on them, named them, and carried them for 3 days through the airport, the pool, the catamaran, and by the sunset. It may sound silly, but it wasn't. Because the saying "don't put all your eggs in one basket" is the one rule founders intentionally break. One idea. One company. One bet that everyone warned us against. Then it gets even more complex. As you begin to grow, you ask others to put THEIR eggs in your basket too: their time, their careers, their trust. That’s the part nobody prepares you for. It’s not just the risk you take on yourself, it’s the responsibility for everyone who believes in you. For 3 days, 199 founders protected one fragile thing and ensured it didn’t crack. 100% survived. It turns out that’s the essence of the job: gather the right people in one place and ensure nothing breaks. That’s what we built Nowadays to do. And today, we’re launching the next chapter! An enterprise-grade Nowadays. The same self-serve, end-to-end AI event planning you already know, now designed to support an entire organization’s worth of eggs. One basket. Big enough for all of them 🥚

how would you get 199 eggs to cancun? pack them in your backpack and hope for the best? without the right protection, the right research, and a team you trust, someone's getting scrambled no egg left behind and here's the thing about eggs: they're fragile. and so is the opportunity. events are not just a to-do list item, they affect real people. the person with a life-threatening allergy who finally felt safe at an event the colleague who almost didn't come but made a lifelong friend. the offsite where someone decided to stay at the company another year. get it wrong and it's forgotten get it right and it becomes a tradition a memory people talk about years later that's the weight of it. and a lot of times this falls on one person. we know firsthand what it looks like when someone tries to juggle all the eggs themselves. the flights, the visa issues, the dietary needs, the room blocks. it only takes one crack. and when you're the one carrying all of it, you can't actually be present for the thing you planned. turns out, to get 199 eggs to cancun without cracking a single one… all you need is the right basket. today we're launching a new chapter of Nowadays . enterprise-grade, and built to carry all your eggs the same AI-powered event planning, now with self-serve so anyone can start without a call.

last week we brought 163 YC founders from 31 batches to Cancun for a YC alumni retreat. the words they used to describe it: electric. unforgettable. family. here's what we learned from pulling it off: 1/ the community is load-bearing. our YC partners pointed out that almost none of YC's billion-dollar companies disappeared after the batch. they stayed connected. they showed up to things. that's not a coincidence. we built this retreat because after the batch ends, that serendipity just stops – and we wanted to bring it back. 2/ the unplanned moments beat the planned ones. the late night mafia games in the presidential suite. the conversations that went until 2am. 100 founders spontaneously belting Linkin Park on a catamaran. we gave people time and space and enough structure to actually talk to each other, and they took it from there. 3/ the people are the product. 92% said they'd come back. but the most common open-ended response wasn't about the venue or the programming. it was about the quality of the founders in the room. that's the thing you can't manufacture. we're doing this again. When travel and meetings live in separate budgets, separate systems, separate conversations with hotels -- real money sits in the gap. Meetings are usually the first thing cut when budgets tighten. But cutting isn't the answer. Visibility is. The companies winning right now aren't spending less -- they're finally seeing the full picture and creating real value from what they already have. I sat in speaker prep today. The energy in that room was something. People who've spent decades on both sides of this problem, buyer and supplier, finally in the same conversation. We won the Y Combinator Call My Agent Hackathon. My teammate Benjamin L. and I built Chief, the first overhearing agent built to work as a chief of staff in live interactions. It listens locally, has intelligent context to your past interactions, and surfaces facts and tool actions when it's necessary. Under the hood, our vision is a customizable framework for overhearing agents. The inspiration came from a report I wrote in a cold email to Penn's Chris Callison-Burch . In a recent paper, he and Andrew Zhu describe a new way of communicating with AI, coined overhearing agents. The thesis is that the traditional chat interface isn't always the best mode. We built Chief for these cases: think high-stakes VC calls, doctor-patient interactions, even casual conversations. Chief runs on four prongs in a continuous loop: the ears, the memory, the decision, the hands. The hands is the action layer with an expandable suite of tool integrations (email, calendar, pull a doc, place a side call), that acts only on the user's own commitments via speaker identity supermemory, and runs on an approval hierarchy so irreversible actions need a yes. Latency was also a big consideration so that retrieval, belief updates, and actions all run in background threads off the hot path. There were plenty of other design choices we'd love to talk about and we are very open to advice and input from those in the space. This weekend, we built a voice for those who have lost theirs. Stephen Hawking was limited to speaking at roughly one word per minute. Technology has improved since then, but accessibility hasn't kept pace.This weekend at NexHacks , my team and I built 𝗛𝗮𝘄𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗜 to close that gap. Using EMG signals and Generative AI, we engineered a high-fidelity neuro-linguistic interface that enables motor-impaired users to communicate at 25 words per minute, an order of magnitude faster than traditional assistive systems, restoring genuine agency rather than merely enabling output. 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 Users communicate via minimal, intentional muscle activations (Right, Down, Select) captured through EMG and mapped onto a semantic grid. Raw signals are "denoised", low-pass filtered, baseline-corrected, and personalized using per-user activation thresholds to reliably separate intent from noise. These commands are streamed in real time to Gemini 2.0 Flash, which predicts intended words using conversational context rather than character-by-character input, and spoken aloud via ElevenLabs, which clones the user’s original voice. The result is not just faster text entry, but a conversational interface that restores agency by translating intent directly into natural speech. 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗱: The system runs on a low-latency, event-driven architecture designed to operate in real time. EMG signals are captured via OpenBCI Ganglion over LSL, processed for intent detection, and routed through a FastAPI + WebSockets backend that coordinates inference, prediction, and audio output. A 60yr old soldering iron, wires stripped from old electronics, 1 paper clip, 3 pen springs, a couple circuitry pieces, and an Arduino. That’s all you need to make a pulse oximeter. For the past couple weeks I have been modeling, 3D printing, soldering, building, and calibrating my own pulse oximeter, which I am proud to say can monitor your blood oxygen and heart rate with 95% accuracy! Using a red and infrared LED, a photodiode measures light absorbance depending on the oxygen saturation and blood flow. The oxygenated vs deoxygenated hemoglobin in your blood absorb red and infrared light differently, which allows the device to estimate blood oxygen saturation, and the pulsatile blood flow allows it to determine heart rate. Simple enough, right? While it may seem technically simple, the most challenging part (and most valuable lesson) wasn’t simply getting the device to work. It was the continual iterations and problem solving to make the mechanical design, software, and technical pieces all work in tandem. During the project, I went through four different designs, two sets of hardware, and was constantly adjusting the system because the real engineering challenge wasn’t it’s creation, it was making the system reliable and repeatable. In the end, this project took me from someone who had never touched a soldering iron and couldn’t tell the difference between a transistor vs resistor, to someone who troubleshooted circuits and code to make a biomedical device on her own. And this is just the beginning.

I found out I was having a daughter right after we closed our pre-seed. My co-founders had already quit their jobs. We had a team whose livelihoods depended on me, and clients whose American dreams depended on Alma . And then: a baby. I remember the panic. What do I do now? I decided to keep going. I'd wanted to build my own company for years, going back to the days I hosted Icons like Dario Amodei in my backyard. And I'd wanted to be a mother for just as long. Both were in my nature. I figured I'd manage. I was wrong. Newborn mom and startup CEO are two of the hardest jobs there are, and I was doing both at once. I cried more times than I can count. I pumped between investor meetings. One day my daughter was sick and wouldn't let go of my hand, so I took my client calls holding her. But the hardest part was never the schedule. It was the guilt. I'd watch other moms talk about the time they spend with their kids, and I'd feel like I was failing. But my husband Chyngyz reframed it for me. He said our daughter won't remember the hours. But she'll grow up watching her mother be resilient, watching how much a woman can carry for the people who depend on her. That's not something I grew up seeing in the culture I come from. It's the whole reason we immigrated to America. So she'll know that in this country, there is nothing she can't achieve and no dream too big to chase. Am I still guilty some days? Yes. But the guilt made me more determined. Every minute away from her is one I owe her to make count. Through Alma I've met so many amazing women who juggle it all, and we don't talk about this part enough. The crying, the guilt, the feeling of failing at both. We perform the easy version and fault ourselves for finding the real one hard. If you're a mom leading at a startup, my DMs are always open. I'd love to know: what's the part nobody warned you about, the part you wish we said out loud more often?

activity.title: Anker and I went through Y Combinator in the summer of 2024. It's one of the best things we've ever done, and I'd recommend it to any early-stage founder. Growing up in Denmark, we had only ever read about Silicon Valley. It felt like a mystical place where people built things we couldn't. YC taught us a lot, but the most important lesson was that we can build something big if we work hard (and smart) enough. That's what gave us the confidence to pivot into AI customer support in the middle of the batch, even though the market was already crowded. Two years (and a lot of late nights) later, Parahelp agents have resolved millions of customer issues for the world’s fastest-growing companies like Cursor and Replit . We'll both be at the YC Internship Expo this Saturday. If you want to help build Parahelp into the leading AI support platform, come talk to us: https://yc.link/r/DcTHZS3h

When your product ships daily, how do you keep an AI support agent up to date? We just released Parahelp automations for support operations tasks like this. Here's how you build an automation that updates your agent whenever relevant parts of your GitHub codebase change.

I’m excited to share that I’m joining Parahelp (YC S24) where I’ll be building their post-sales function - the Customer Acceleration team. Parahelp is the #1 solution for fast moving tech companies that want to automate their customer support & operations workflows with AI. Some of the coolest companies out there like Cursor , Lovable , Replit & Supabase already use Parahelp today! Interested in joining that list of cool companies or simply want to learn more about the product or the team? Shoot me a dm! PS: Always looking for great talent that’s up for a challenge 😜

If a tool has an API, you can connect it to your AI support agent by chatting with Parahelp . Here's how I build a Linear connection so our support agent can handle feature requests the same way we do.

Lots of other AI support solutions are now claiming to be self-improving. By this, they mean once their AI makes a mistake (in production), then it might learn from it. They don't mean proactively in the moment when something changes. This is a minor issue for companies that rarely change such as hotels or airlines (which is what they’re built for), but it makes it completely broken for startups where things constantly change. Given how fast our customers evolve at Parahelp , we’ve built Parahelp to proactively change when your company does. This includes company announcements in Slack, new PRs being merged in GitHub, Notion page updates, Linear tickets, and much much more. Learning from your mistakes is great, but overrated. Proactively learning when your company evolves is the only way to actually provide delightful customer experiences at fast-moving startups.

Today, we're launching Parahelp 3. Intelligence is no longer the bottleneck for AI resolving support tickets - context and tool connections are. Parahelp 3 solves both: - Automations that update your AI support agent whenever your product and policies change - Coding capabilities that let Parahelp build reliable, scoped connections to any tool with an API You build and run your AI support agent on Parahelp to resolve even your most complex tickets end-to-end. Thanks to everyone who has helped us get this far. We're very excited about the next chapter! Read more in the comments.

Expedite has been helping the Parahelp (YC S24) team expand to the US. Parahelp is already trusted by teams like Perplexity, Cursor and Replit, and backed by an $18M Series A led by Alt Capital with participation from Y Combinator and Hanabi Capital. Helping founders like this build in the US is the whole reason we started Expedite. SF is lucky to have you. congrats team 🚀

My biggest concern when I first thought about joining Parahelp was the market. Anker and Mads were so obviously impressive, but customer support seemed like arguably the single worst market to enter. Seemingly half of the latest YC cohorts had been AI customer support solutions, competitors were well-funded, and everyone had recognised it as a great market - clearly the market was lost already. It took me a bit to fully internalise, but none of the other AI customer support solutions actually work for fast-moving tech companies. This might sound ludicrous to anyone who hasn’t tried them, but it is obviously true for anyone who has. Typically this doesn't materialise in direct dislike of the tools, but more “XYZ tool is great, it just doesn’t work for us since we don’t have time to set it up, keep it up to date, and using our tools is too complex.” This is because customer support in tech is a completely different role compared to non-tech, which was immediately evident when I actually went and talked with support leaders. Other solutions fail for two reasons 1. Things constantly change. New launches lead to new bugs, features, and edge cases. If this needs to be manually changed, reviewed, and tested - then your solution will fail immediately. 2. Needs are much more complex. The average support ticket involves looking up customer information in different systems, making a judgment based on the information, and performing actions in different tools. At Parahelp, we have deliberately chosen only to work with fast-moving tech companies. No airlines, hotels, or ecommerce. Instead, we focused entirely on the fastest-moving companies with the most complex tickets. Today, this includes Cursor , Lovable , Perplexity , Replit , Framer , Supabase , Fyxer , HeyGen , Speak , Public , OpusClip , bolt.new , Conductor , Mintlify , and many more. For our customers, we solve up to 92% of all customer support tickets end-to-end. We're able to do this since Parahelp uses your tools to look up customer information (e.g. Datadog logs), perform actions (e.g. issue a refund, change your account settings), and automatically keep itself up to date as your product changes (e.g. updating configurations when you merge a PR in GitHub ). Think your customer interactions are too complex? Drop me a DM.

projects.title: Modeling the Male Adult Nerve Cord of The Drosophila Melanogaster Using Spiking Neural Networks
projects.description: Recent literature in the field of neuronal locomotion has been able to successfully map the ventral nerve cord (VNC) of the male Drosophila Melanogaster in a public data set that offers a robust connectome of the VNC. This research project seeks to model the data found in the Male Adult Nerve Cord (MANC), utilizing a differential equation-based, spiking neural network model (SNNs). With over 23,000 neurons, this model is based on the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) that is used to simulate neurons due to its biological realism and computational efficiency. By having a full data set and mapping the over 5.3 million different synaptic connections, researchers will be able to automate the mapping process of local neuron circuits when they experiment with silencing or simulating certain neurons. This project ultimately aims to create an exploratory tool that will enable researchers to better understand the underlying functional architecture of the MANC. Our model demonstrates the viability of continuing to model the Drosophila's nervous system through the connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identities of neurons alone, and the ability to yield hypotheses that are experimentally verifiable.

RL-style environments are powerful, but they’re hard to understand and even harder to document. After working with Muhib Waqar , we started thinking about how much product knowledge is locked inside PDFs. PRDs, specs, and design docs carry intent, decisions, and tradeoffs, but machines mostly see them as raw text. So we built a small experiment on top of NVIDIA nv-ingest → https://lnkd.in/gUG5APNf nv-ingest is an open-source document extraction pipeline designed for RAG workflows. It orchestrates OCR, layout detection, tables, and structure, and connects to NVIDIA NIM microservices for multimodal understanding. We used it to process a real Amazon PRD, generated structured JSON (text, tables, images, layout), and wrote a reasoning framework ( claude.md , cursor.md ) to see whether an AI could reconstruct a product spec from structured data alone. From JSON alone, the system was able to extract requirements, personas, user journeys, UI flows, system structure, and even surface gaps in the original PRD. What surprised me wasn’t that it worked, but how close the reconstructed spec was to the original. It felt less like “document parsing” and more like treating PRDs as data that systems can reason over. If this approach improves, PRD updates could be ingested continuously, reducing cognitive overhead for engineers and PMs and making product knowledge easier to operationalize 🧠 ...more

Three years ago I did my first internship at a research lab in a children's hospital. It wasn't really aligned with the engineering and PM work I wanted. I was running samples, gathering data for experiments, and using software I thought I'd never touch again. But I took the job because it was the only one that said yes. Fast forward to my first product role, at a company building AI tools for lab scientists. As I was doing customer interviews and trying to understand these scientists' pain points, I had such a clear picture of what they were talking about. When they brought up their software, instrumentation, and the tiny issues eating up their day, I could put myself in their shoes by channelling my earlier research role. I felt like an engineer who understood the science and could make a real impact. It reminded me of Steve Jobs' quote: "You cannot connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backward." Because when you're young and trying to make a name for yourself, you think that unless every minute is spent in the perfect role, you're automatically falling behind. And the truth is you're not. You just need to collect as many dots as possible, knowing that future you will connect them all together. If you're early in your career and can't see how what you're doing now fits into where you're going, it probably doesn't need to make sense yet. Just keep collecting. #CareerJourney #ConnectTheDots #ProductManagement #EarlyCareer

“Find your passion” might be the worst, yet most often parroted piece of advice ever. It’s an incredible feeling, but it won’t be there for you when the chips are down; you’re facing failure and rejection; and you feel like you just can’t get anything right. Just ask any repeatedly successful person and they’ll tell you that what got them through their lows was the discipline, determination, and support from others to build something to completion and see it through. And it’s because when you’re betting on yourself, the biggest risk you take isn’t failing, but rather not failing enough. If you stop a quarter of the way through, when the dopamine rush is nowhere to be found and suddenly it’s not fun any more, you’ll always leave lessons on the table. Building and, subsequently, launching will always be worth it if you’re able to maximize your learning. And lest we all forget Master Yoda’s words: The greatest teacher, failure is. So, think of passion as a reward and draw your energy and motivation from something that is far better suited to pushing through. And follow along Lucas Chan ’s journey of betting on himself!

🇨🇦 AMD is buying Toronto's Taalas. Terms were not disclosed, and it still needs regulatory approval. Taalas was founded in 2023 by three former AMD employees who had been leaders at Tenstorrent. It raised $169 million USD in February and had taken about $219 million USD in total. The idea was to hardwire a trained model straight into silicon rather than run it on general-purpose GPUs. AMD says the technology goes into its accelerator roadmap. Look at AMD's year. MK1 in November, MEXT in June, FastFlowLM in July, Taalas now. Four inference deals in nine months, and Taalas is the second Canadian one after it took the Untether AI team in 2025. None of these had meaningful revenue yet. What is being bought is design talent, and it is concentrating into two or three balance sheets very quickly. The Toronto part is what I keep noticing. Untether's team went to AMD. Nvidia acquired CentML. Tenstorrent, founded here, is headquartered in Santa Clara. Ottawa's Hyperlume went to San Jose's Credo, and an SEC filing later showed the price was $92 million USD. AMD has had people here since it bought Markham's ATI in 2006. Four Canadian chip companies in two years. There was no Canadian buyer in any of them, and I would like to know whether one was ever asked.

July was my last month at Kodiak . The past 8 years have been exciting and incredibly rewarding. I started about 5 weeks after the company was founded with nothing but a laptop and a rack full of snacks, and led the company as CTO to the first full commercial launch of a driverless trucking fleet - 24/7 operations, owned and operated by the customer - in 2024, followed by Kodiak’s public listing on NASDAQ in 2025. As of June 2026, Kodiak had 35 driverless trucks deployed at the customer’s site, having operated 40,000+ cumulative paid hours without anyone in the cabin. The latest software release further increased efficiency by 30%, all in a harsh environment with oncoming, third-party traffic. And it also isn’t just the one vehicle, because not all customers want the same: we built several driverless platforms, from big semis to offroad vehicles, that could operate safely in their respective environments. Most recently, the team delivered the first driverless daycab that I know of, on yet another new OEM base platform and with a new Gen7 generation of autonomy hardware. This isn’t just technology, it’s a full product that is actually useful to customers - and that product focus has been in Kodiak’s DNA from day one. Behind the scenes, the reality of Physical AI is amazingly complex: It took designing a system from the ground up that could meet the rigor of a full safety assessment to launch in 2024 and repeatedly after; finding and hiring hundreds of excellent people to refine and execute the plan; coordinating OEMs, suppliers, contract manufacturers, and partners around the world and earning their trust over years; real-world testing in both hot and icy conditions from the Permian to Michigan, and many interstates between; testing in simulated environments that reflect all of those conditions with well understood fidelity; and aligning the software, hardware, and systems engineering so we could operate safely and efficiently at the same time. I was part of it at every step, leading, helping, and motivating; but the real credit goes to the team at Kodiak who did the hard work on the ground and made it happen. I keep being impressed by what this team is able to do, often on tight timelines and tighter budgets. I’ve seen first hand how listening well, sharing insights, and helping others grow will exponentially increase the impact of an organization. Thank you for giving me the opportunity and trust to lead you through the ups and downs every startup goes through on the way to success. It’s been an incredible experience! Now it’s time to make space for the next generation of leaders at Kodiak. I've been enjoying time with family, both here in the US and in Austria, and reconnecting with people I haven't had a chance to talk to for way too long. If you're around, let's chat - I'd love to catch up.
